quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: I said Tuesday, not Thursday.
quests.textToSpeak: I said Tuesday, not Thursday.
options: Peak on 'said' — the speaker is repeating a statement
Peaks on 'Tuesday' and 'Thursday' — the two days are contrasted
quests.correctAnswer: Peaks on 'Tuesday' and 'Thursday' — the two days are contrasted
quests.hint: Two days are compared in one sentence. Listen for which words the speaker pushes out of the background.
quests.explanation: When two items are set against each other, both carry extra pitch height and force. 'Said' stays low because the real issue is which day, not whether it was said.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Contrast puts a pitch peak on each of the two competing words.

quests.instruction: The barista brought a small cup, but you ordered a large one. Which word gets the peak when you correct it?
quests.word: I asked for a large coffee.
quests.textToSpeak: I asked for a large coffee.
options: Peak on 'large' — the size is wrong
Peak on 'coffee' — the drink is wrong
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'large' — the size is wrong
quests.hint: Ask yourself what was actually wrong with the order. The peak follows the problem.
quests.explanation: The mistake is the size, so 'large' carries the peak. 'Coffee' is fine, so it is delivered with less energy and the pitch drops after it.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 The peak goes on the word that fixes the mistake.

quests.instruction: The airline gave you an aisle seat, but you booked a window seat. Which word will you stress when you speak to the agent?
quests.word: I reserved a window seat.
quests.textToSpeak: I reserved a window seat.
options: Peak on 'window' — what was booked
Peak on 'reserved' — what you did
quests.hint: Decide what the agent needs to notice first. Where does the disagreement sit?
quests.explanation: The type of seat is the disputed detail, so 'window' takes the peak. 'Reserved' is background, since nobody disputes that you booked something.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Stress the disputed word so the listener hears where the error is.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: No, I booked a hotel.
quests.textToSpeak: No, I booked a hotel.
options: Peak on 'hotel' — the new information
Peak on 'booked' — the repeated action
quests.hint: A friend has just asked, 'Did you book a flight?' Which part of your reply is new to them?
quests.explanation: 'Booked' was already implied by the question, so it stays quiet. The new piece is 'hotel', and that word carries the peak and the final fall.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 New information gets the peak; repeated information fades.

quests.instruction: Your manager asks, 'Who broke the printer?' Which word carries the peak in your answer?
quests.word: Marco broke it.
quests.textToSpeak: Marco broke it.
options: Peak on 'broke' — the action
Peak on 'Marco' — the answer to 'who'
quests.hint: Think about what the manager wants to find out. That word is where your voice should rise.
quests.explanation: The question already established that something was broken, so 'broke' is given. 'Marco' is the missing information and takes the peak.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 The word that answers the question carries the peak.

quests.instruction: A colleague asks, 'Where is the spare key?' Which word gets the peak in your answer?
quests.word: It's under the flowerpot.
quests.textToSpeak: It's under the flowerpot.
options: Peak on 'flowerpot' — the location
Peak on 'under' — the position
quests.hint: The question asked 'where', so ask which word answers it best.
quests.explanation: The answer to 'where' is a location, so 'flowerpot' takes the pitch. 'Under' is part of the answer but less surprising, so it stays lower.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 A 'where' answer places the peak on the place word.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: It wasn't Priya who called, it was Daniel.
quests.textToSpeak: It wasn't Priya who called, it was Daniel.
options: Peak on 'called' — whether the call happened is disputed
Peaks on 'Priya' and 'Daniel' — the names are contrasted
quests.correctAnswer: Peaks on 'Priya' and 'Daniel' — the names are contrasted
quests.hint: Listen for which two words carry the biggest pitch movement.
quests.explanation: The correction is about who made the call, so both names take peaks. 'Called' is agreed by both sides and stays low.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 In a correction, both the wrong and the right item stand out.

quests.instruction: A coworker says the seminar is in Room 5. It's actually Room 15. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: It's in Room fifteen.
quests.textToSpeak: It's in Room fifteen.
options: Peak on 'Room' — the place type is corrected
Peak on 'fifteen' — the number is corrected
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'fifteen' — the number is corrected
quests.hint: Only one part of your coworker's statement was wrong. Decide which.
quests.explanation: The number is the error, so 'fifteen' takes the peak. In numbers like this, the stress falls on the last syllable to separate 'fifteen' from 'fifty'.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Correct the number, and stress its final syllable for -teen numbers.

quests.instruction: Your friend thinks you're allergic to peanuts, but it is shellfish. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: I'm allergic to shellfish.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm allergic to shellfish.
options: Peak on 'allergic' — the condition is corrected
Peak on 'shellfish' — the allergy is corrected
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'shellfish' — the allergy is corrected
quests.hint: Your friend already has the condition right. What did they get wrong?
quests.explanation: Your friend was right that you have an allergy, so 'allergic' stays quiet. 'Shellfish' is the correction and gets the peak and the fall.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Leave the correct part quiet and push the corrected part.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: Anna didn't drive to the airport.
quests.textToSpeak: Anna didn't drive to the airport.
options: Peak on 'Anna' — someone else drove
Peak on 'airport' — she drove elsewhere
quests.hint: The speaker is contradicting an assumption. Which part of the assumption is being denied?
quests.explanation: A peak on 'Anna' suggests someone else did the driving. A peak on 'airport' would suggest she drove somewhere different. The words are identical, but the stress changes the message.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 The stressed word in a denial shows what is being denied.

quests.instruction: You promised to buy coffee, and someone says you promised to pay for dinner. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: I never promised to pay for dinner.
quests.textToSpeak: I never promised to pay for dinner.
options: Peak on 'dinner' — the promise was about something else
Peak on 'promised' — no promise was ever made
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'dinner' — the promise was about something else
quests.hint: The speaker denies only part of the claim. Work out which part.
quests.explanation: Stressing 'dinner' means 'I promised something, just not that'. Stressing 'promised' would deny making any promise at all, which isn't what you mean.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Stress in a denial points to the part that is wrong, not the whole statement.

quests.instruction: Your colleague told the team the price but skipped you. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: She didn't tell me the price.
quests.textToSpeak: She didn't tell me the price.
options: Peak on 'price' — I heard other details
Peak on 'me' — others were told
quests.hint: Who is missing from the group that was informed? Listen for that word.
quests.explanation: The complaint is that you were left out, so 'me' takes the peak. If 'price' were stressed, it would imply you were told everything except the price.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Stress a pronoun to say 'not me, but others'.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: The meeting is at fifteen, not fifty.
quests.textToSpeak: The meeting is at fifteen, not fifty.
options: Peaks on 'fifteen' and 'fifty' — the numbers are contrasted
Peak on 'meeting' — the event itself is being contrasted
quests.correctAnswer: Peaks on 'fifteen' and 'fifty' — the numbers are contrasted
quests.hint: Similar-sounding numbers are easy to confuse. Listen to which words receive the strongest pitch.
quests.explanation: Numbers that sound alike need clear peaks, and -teen numbers stress the last syllable while -ty numbers stress the first. This helps listeners avoid a costly mistake.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Peak on similar-sounding numbers to protect the listener from confusion.

quests.instruction: You are confirming a gate change on the phone. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: Flight two-one-four leaves from Gate B, not Gate D.
quests.textToSpeak: Flight two-one-four leaves from Gate B, not Gate D.
options: Peak on 'leaves' — the departure is stressed
Peaks on 'B' and 'D' — the gates are contrasted
quests.correctAnswer: Peaks on 'B' and 'D' — the gates are contrasted
quests.hint: The confusion could be between two letters. Decide which words must be crystal clear.
quests.explanation: The letters B and D sound similar, so both must be delivered with a higher peak. 'Leaves' is not in dispute and stays low.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Letters that sound alike need extra height and clarity.

quests.instruction: Your teammate thought the deadline was midnight, but it's earlier. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: The deadline is Friday at noon, not midnight.
quests.textToSpeak: The deadline is Friday at noon, not midnight.
options: Peak on 'Friday' — the day of the deadline is contrasted
Peak on 'noon' and 'midnight' — the times are contrasted
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'noon' and 'midnight' — the times are contrasted
quests.hint: The day is not in dispute. Which words show the real difference?
quests.explanation: 'Noon' and 'midnight' are the two competing times, so they carry the peaks. 'Friday' is old information, so it stays lower.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Peak the contrasted times, not the shared day.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: Only Sam knew about the surprise.
quests.textToSpeak: Only Sam knew about the surprise.
options: Peak on 'surprise' — the surprise is the issue
Peak on 'Only' and 'Sam' — nobody else knew
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'Only' and 'Sam' — nobody else knew
quests.hint: The word 'only' points at something. Listen for the word that follows it.
quests.explanation: 'Only' links to 'Sam', so both carry emphasis. This tells the listener that Sam is the exception, not the surprise.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 'Only' points its peak at the word it limits.

quests.instruction: A colleague is surprised that someone arrived late. Which pattern fits?
quests.word: Even the manager arrived late.
quests.textToSpeak: Even the manager arrived late.
options: Peak on 'Even' and 'manager' — surprising person
Peak on 'late' — the lateness is surprising
quests.hint: 'Even' suggests an extreme case. Decide which person is the extreme case.
quests.explanation: 'Even' works with 'manager' because the manager is the least expected person to be late. The stress signals the surprise.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 'Even' adds a peak to the least expected item.

quests.instruction: You want to make clear that you didn't order two desserts. Which word will you stress?
quests.word: I only ordered one dessert.
quests.textToSpeak: I only ordered one dessert.
options: Peak on 'one' — the quantity
Peak on 'dessert' — the item
quests.hint: Think about what was over-counted. That word carries the message.
quests.explanation: The correction is about quantity, so 'one' takes the peak. 'Dessert' is stated but is not in dispute.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Peak on the number to correct a quantity.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: Did you say the second floor?
quests.textToSpeak: Did you say the second floor?
options: Peak on 'second' with a final rise — checking the number
Peak on 'say' with a final rise — checking whether she spoke
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'second' with a final rise — checking the number
quests.hint: You heard 'third floor' earlier and now hear something else. Focus on which word is under question.
quests.explanation: The doubt is about the floor number, so 'second' carries the peak. The final rise keeps the question open for confirmation.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯📈 In a checking question, peak the doubtful word and rise at the end.

quests.instruction: There are several folders on a desk and you point at one. Which pattern fits your question?
quests.word: Is this the folder you meant?
quests.textToSpeak: Is this the folder you meant?
options: Peak on 'meant' with a final rise — asking about intention
Peak on 'this' with a final rise — picking one from several
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'this' with a final rise — picking one from several
quests.hint: You are trying to pick out one object from a group. Which word does that job?
quests.explanation: 'This' picks out one folder among many, so it gets a peak. A gentle rise at the end asks for confirmation.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯📈 Stress the picking word, then rise for the question.

quests.instruction: You sent the wrong file and want your coworker to use another. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: Could you review the final draft instead?
quests.textToSpeak: Could you review the final draft instead?
options: Peak on 'review' — the action changes
Peak on 'final' — replaces the earlier file
quests.correctAnswer: Peak on 'final' — replaces the earlier file
quests.hint: Which word makes the difference between your two files?
quests.explanation: 'Final' separates this file from the earlier one, so it takes the peak. The rise on 'instead' keeps the request polite.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯📈 Put the peak on the word that separates the two files, and keep the polite rise.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: I didn't say it was bad, I said it was expensive.
quests.textToSpeak: I didn't say it was bad, I said it was expensive.
options: Peaks on 'bad' and 'expensive' — contrasted judgments
Peaks on 'say' and 'said' — the speech act is contested
quests.hint: Two claims are set against each other. Listen for the two words that stand out.
quests.explanation: The speaker isn't denying that they spoke, they are denying the word 'bad'. So 'bad' and 'expensive' carry the peaks.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 The words that differ between the two clauses take the peaks.

quests.instruction: You explain your reaction to a gift. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: It's not that I don't like it, I just can't afford it.
quests.textToSpeak: It's not that I don't like it, I just can't afford it.
options: Peaks on 'not' and 'just' — the negations
Peaks on 'like' and 'afford' — contrasted reasons
quests.hint: The speaker wants to clarify a reason. Which two words hold the contrast?
quests.explanation: 'Like' and 'afford' are the real alternatives. The negation words are grammatical glue and stay lower.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Stress the contrasted reasons, not the connector words.

quests.instruction: A manager corrects how a plan is described. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: We're not cutting the budget, we're reallocating it.
quests.textToSpeak: We're not cutting the budget, we're reallocating it.
options: Peaks on 'cutting' and 'reallocating' — reframed action
Peaks on 'budget' and 'it' — the object being contrasted
quests.hint: The object is the same in both halves. What changes?
quests.explanation: Since 'budget' and 'it' refer to the same thing, they stay quiet. The change is the verb, so 'cutting' and 'reallocating' peak.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Repeated words fade when the contrast is in the verb.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: Not that bag, this one.
quests.textToSpeak: Not that bag, this one.
options: Peaks on 'that' and 'this' — the two bags
Peak on 'bag' — the object type
quests.correctAnswer: Peaks on 'that' and 'this' — the two bags
quests.hint: You point at two bags in a shop. Which words help the listener see which one you mean?
quests.explanation: Pointing words 'that' and 'this' carry the contrast, while 'bag' is already known. Speakers often lift the pitch to match a gesture.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Pointing words are natural focus words.

quests.instruction: A shop has two sizes on display. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: I'll take the smaller one, please.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll take the smaller one, please.
options: Peak on 'smaller' — choosing between sizes
Peak on 'take' — deciding to buy
quests.hint: You've already decided to buy. What is the new information?
quests.explanation: The decision to buy is background. The choice of size is the new part, so 'smaller' takes the peak.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Peak the choice, not the decision to choose.

quests.instruction: An invoice was sent to the wrong person. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: Please send it to accounting, not to me.
quests.textToSpeak: Please send it to accounting, not to me.
options: Peak on 'send' — the action being corrected here
Peaks on 'accounting' and 'me' — the recipients
quests.hint: The action isn't in dispute. Who should receive it?
quests.explanation: The confusion is about who should receive the invoice, so 'accounting' and 'me' carry the peaks. 'Send' is agreed.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯 Contrast the recipients, not the action.

quests.instruction: Identify the intonation
quests.word: We packed sandwiches, fruit, and plenty of water.
quests.textToSpeak: We packed sandwiches, fruit, and plenty of water.
options: Fall on every item — separate statements
Rise, rise, fall — list complete
quests.hint: Recall the pattern for lists. Listen to how the three items relate.
quests.explanation: The first two items lift to keep the list open, and 'water' falls to close it. This reviews the list pattern from earlier levels.
quests.pitchRule: ↗️📉 Lift the items, fall on the last.

quests.instruction: A friend thinks your flight is on Sunday. Which pattern fits your correction?
quests.word: My flight is on Saturday.
quests.textToSpeak: My flight is on Saturday.
options: Peak on 'flight' — corrects the topic
Peak on 'Saturday' — corrects the day
quests.hint: Your friend has the right topic. Which detail did they get wrong?
quests.explanation: 'Flight' is agreed and stays quiet. 'Saturday' is the corrected detail and takes the peak and the fall.
quests.pitchRule: 🎯📉 The corrected word gets the peak, and the sentence lands on it.

quests.instruction: You finish an email request out loud. Which pattern will you use?
quests.word: If you can, please bring the signed form.
quests.textToSpeak: If you can, please bring the signed form.
options: Rise on 'can', fall on 'form'
Fall on 'can', fall on 'form'
quests.hint: There is an opening condition and a main request. Decide where the boundary lies.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause is only the setup, so it lifts on 'can'. The main request falls on 'form'. It reviews thought groups and requests together.
quests.pitchRule: ↗️📉 Softeners lift, the request falls.
